verified_ref: Adhyatma Upanishad 15 (our number; see note). The same shloka is Vivekachudamani 324 (Madhavananda numbering), in its section on heedlessness (pramāda).
attribution_note: The Adhyatma has no dialogue frame; its closing names a lineage (Apantaratama to Brahma to Ghora Angiras to Raikva to Rama). 'Seer / Seeker' is a fair generic label. Aiyar notes it is also called the Turiyatita Avadhuta Upanishad.
translation_note: Accurate. Shaivala is moss/sedge/water-weed; parāṅmukha = turned away (Madhavananda: averse to meditation on the Self). Verse number not independently checked against a numbered Sanskrit edition (sanskritdocuments.org showed a bot check, so it was not used). Its position in K. Narayanasvami Aiyar's 1914 translation fits this number.
context: Just before, the text says the knower must not allow even a moment's carelessness in abiding in Brahman, which the wise call death itself. This verse gives the image; the next says one who reaches the state of the Alone in life stays so after the body falls, and urges constant samadhi.

key_terms.sense: illusion, the covering power of ignorance

core_teaching: Clarity is not won once; like weed closing back over a pond, confusion returns the moment even a wise person stops attending.

commentaries.who: K. Narayanasvami Aiyar, Thirty Minor Upanishads (1914), surrounding text
commentaries.gist: Placed after the warning that carelessness in abiding in Brahman is death itself; the moss image shows that maya re-covers even the wise who are careless for a moment.

commentaries.who: Vivekachudamani (attrib. Shankara), tr. Madhavananda (1921), same verse with translator's note
commentaries.gist: Madhavananda's note: the weed must be held back with a bamboo or the like; in the same way, ongoing meditation is needed to keep ignorance away.

practical_reading: Insight fades if not practised; keep a daily practice going because old patterns close back in quickly.
misreadings: Not 'you will always fall back, so why try'
Not a reason for anxious self-monitoring
cautions: Can feed guilt in someone who has 'slipped' (relapse, broken habit); frame as care, not failure
speaks_to: keeping a meditation or prayer practice
not_for: someone harshly self-critical after a relapse
research_note: No classical bhashya on the Adhyatma was available (Upanishad Brahmayogin's commentary not found online). Commentary entries are the surrounding text in translation and the translator's note on the Vivekachudamani parallel.

verified_ref: Adhyatma Upanishad 47 (our number; see note). The same shloka is Vivekachudamani 440 (Madhavananda), whose last word reads jīvanmukta-lakṣaṇaḥ ('is the mark of one free in life') instead of jīvanmukta iṣyate.
attribution_note: No dialogue frame; generic label fine.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Harassed' renders pīḍyamāne (tormented); Madhavananda specifies it is the body that is worshipped or tormented. Verse number not independently checked against a numbered Sanskrit edition (sanskritdocuments.org showed a bot check, so it was not used). Its position in K. Narayanasvami Aiyar's 1914 translation fits this number.
context: One of a run of definitions of the jivanmukta, the one free while living: no 'I' in body and senses, no 'other' in anything else, no difference seen between self, Brahman and world, and evenness whether honoured or reviled. The text then turns to prarabdha karma.
core_teaching: The mark of inner freedom is staying the same whether the good honour you or the wicked torment you.

commentaries.who: K. Narayanasvami Aiyar, Thirty Minor Upanishads (1914), surrounding text
commentaries.gist: Listed among marks of the jivanmukta: one who keeps equanimity whether revered by the good or reviled by the vicious, next to having no sense of 'I' in the body and no sense of difference.

commentaries.who: Vivekachudamani (attrib. Shankara), tr. Madhavananda (1921), same verse with translator's note
commentaries.gist: The same verse in the Vivekachudamani describes one who feels the same whether his body is worshipped or tormented, as the mark of one liberated in life.

practical_reading: Praise and criticism both pull at us; practising evenness toward both is a sign of inner freedom, and a goal to grow into.
misreadings: Not a call to tolerate abuse or stay in harmful situations
Not indifference to justice or to others' suffering
cautions: For someone being harassed or abused, 'stay the same' can sound like 'put up with it'; describes an inner state, not a rule about staying
not_for: someone currently experiencing abuse or bullying
research_note: No classical bhashya available; commentary entries are the translation context and the Vivekachudamani parallel.

verified_ref: Adhyatma Upanishad 53-54 (our numbers; see note). The same two shlokas are Vivekachudamani 451-452 (Madhavananda).
attribution_note: No dialogue frame; generic label fine.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Gomatau' = in the belief that it is a cow. Verse number not independently checked against a numbered Sanskrit edition (sanskritdocuments.org showed a bot check, so it was not used). Its position in K. Narayanasvami Aiyar's 1914 translation fits this number.
context: The text has just said that knowing 'I am Brahman' burns up karma stored from countless past births, as waking ends the deeds of a dream. Here it qualifies that: prarabdha, the karma that already began this body, still runs its course. It then goes further: for one who truly knows the Self as beyond birth and death, prarabdha does not touch him, and the Veda speaks of it only for those who doubt.

key_terms.sense: karma already in motion, which shaped this life

core_teaching: Knowledge does not stop consequences already set in motion; like a released arrow, they play out, even once you see things differently.

commentaries.who: K. Narayanasvami Aiyar, Thirty Minor Upanishads (1914), surrounding text
commentaries.gist: Follows the claim that 'I am Brahman' destroys stored karma; the arrow aimed at a supposed tiger still strikes the cow. The text adds that for one who knows the Self as unborn, prarabdha has no real hold.

commentaries.who: Vivekachudamani (attrib. Shankara), tr. Madhavananda (1921), same verse with translator's note
commentaries.gist: Work that shaped this body is not destroyed by knowledge before yielding fruit; prarabdha is spent by experience, while stored and future karma burn in knowledge (VC 451-453).

practical_reading: Changing your understanding doesn't instantly undo the effects of past choices; let them play out with patience instead of self-blame.
misreadings: Not fatalism: it concerns only what has already begun
Not a claim that the person deserved their suffering
cautions: Karma language can feel blaming to someone suffering illness, loss or injustice
Hunting imagery
speaks_to: living with the consequences of past decisions
after a change of heart, when life hasn't caught up
not_for: someone suffering illness, abuse or loss who may hear 'it's your karma'
research_note: No classical bhashya available; commentary entries are the translation context and the Vivekachudamani parallel.

verified_ref: Aitareya Upanishad 2.1.4 (= GRETIL 'aitup 2.4'; part of Aitareya Aranyaka II.5.1).
attribution_note: No named speaker; narrator is fine.
translation_note: Accurate. The Sanskrit speaks of a father and son ('this self of his', the son, is set in the father's place). Our 'the child' and 'the parent' make it gender-neutral, a reasonable choice for the app; note that 'good works' = puṇyebhyaḥ karmabhyaḥ, the scripturally enjoined duties.
context: Chapter 2 of the Aitareya gives a person three births: as seed passing to the mother, as the child born and raised, and, after handing over his duties to the son and dying, as rebirth. This is the third. The chapter closes with the sage Vamadeva, who knew all his births while still in the womb and, rising above, became immortal (2.1.5-6).

key_terms.sense: one who has done what was to be done

core_teaching: The child takes up the parent's work; the parent, duties done and grown old, dies and is born again. Father and son are treated as one self across the generations.

commentaries.gist: The son takes the father's place for enjoined duties (citing Brihadaranyaka 1.5.17). The father, debts paid and aged, dies and takes a new body by his karma. It is the son's 'third birth' because father and son are one self.

practical_reading: Handing on responsibilities to the next generation is part of a full life; it can be read as permission to let go once your part is done.
misreadings: Not 'children exist to carry on the parent's agenda'
Not a statement that only sons count
cautions: About aging, death and rebirth; the parent's death is the 'third birth'
Avoid for someone whose parent has just died or is dying unless they seek it
Can sting for bereaved parents or the childless
speaks_to: adult children taking on family roles
not_for: fresh grief for a parent
bereaved parents
people struggling with infertility
research_note: Only Shankara's Sanskrit commentary was read (GRETIL). Müller's SBE 1 translation of Aitareya Aranyaka II.5 was not checked for this verse.

verified_ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 1.3.28 (Kanva recension; last paragraph of the Udgitha Brahmana). Same number in Madhavananda, Hume and Vasu/Madhva. (wisdomlib's heading misprints it as 1.13.28.)
attribution_note: No named speaker; the text prescribes what the sacrificer (yajamana) mutters while the Prastotri priest begins the chant. 'Seer' is acceptable.
translation_note: Fair. Hume makes clear the sacrificer, not the priest, mutters the three lines. The verse goes on to explain each line (unreal = death, darkness = death, light/real = immortality) and to say the chanter may then win food and boons by singing; our translation stops after the prayer.
context: Chapter 1.3 tells how the gods chose the vital breath (prana) as their chanter because it alone could not be pierced by evil. This closing paragraph gives a practice for one who knows that teaching: during the Pavamana chants the sacrificer mutters the three-line prayer, and the Upanishad glosses it at once. The rest of the paragraph turns to winning food and wishes through the remaining chants.

key_terms.sense: lead me from the unreal (asat) to the real (sat)
lead me from darkness to light
lead me from death to deathlessness
the 'ascending' recitation, a mantra repetition that raises the reciter

core_teaching: The text itself says all three lines mean one thing: 'make me immortal'. Unreal and darkness both stand for death; real and light for immortality.

commentaries.gist: A japa prescribed for one who knows the vital-breath meditation; its fruit is rising to divinity. Shankara takes death as ordinary ignorant thought and action, and the immortal as one's divine nature; the third line sums up the first two.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu, SBH vol. 14 (1916)
commentaries.gist: Madhva restricts the prayer to a special class of souls destined to serve as vehicles of Vayu, who recite it while meditating on Vishnu; it is addressed to Vishnu as the one who leads out of sorrow.

practical_reading: Teachers use it as a short daily prayer for moving from confusion and fear toward clarity; the Upanishad's own gloss lets a reader treat all three lines as one wish to outgrow what dies.
misreadings: Not a general invocation detached from practice: in the text it is a japa within a chant, glossed by the Upanishad itself
Not a prayer for a long physical life; 'immortality' here is the deathless, not avoiding death
cautions: 'Death' is named twice in the gloss; fine for most readers but can jar in fresh bereavement if the gloss is quoted
speaks_to: starting a new day or practice
not_for: someone wanting a prayer for a sick person's recovery (the 'immortality' is not bodily survival)

verified_ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 1.4.2 (Kanva). Same in Madhavananda, Hume, Vasu/Madhva.
attribution_note: Narrative; no speaker. Shankara identifies 'he' as Viraj, the first embodied being; Madhva as Brahma (the four-faced creator).
translation_note: Accurate.
context: 1.4 opens with the Self alone in the beginning, looking around and seeing nothing but itself, and saying 'I am'. Here that first being feels fear, reasons it away, and fear leaves. Next (1.4.3) he feels no delight alone, longs for a second, and divides into husband and wife, from whom creatures come.

key_terms.sense: one who is alone is afraid
fear comes only from a second

core_teaching: Fear depends on there being something other than oneself; when the first being saw there was nothing besides him, fear dissolved. The Advaita reading takes this as fear born of ignorance and cured by knowing oneness.

commentaries.gist: Viraj feared just as we do, from a false notion that he could be destroyed. Right knowledge of the Self removed it, since a second entity that causes fear is only projected by ignorance.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu, SBH vol. 14 (1916)
commentaries.gist: The being is Brahma, who feared from lack of discrimination; he reasoned that no equal exists, his only superior (Vishnu) loves him as a father, and everything lower is under his control, so fear left.

practical_reading: Much anxiety is about what we imagine standing against us; looking straight at the fear and asking 'what exactly am I afraid of?' can loosen it.
misreadings: Not 'you should be alone to be fearless'
Not a dismissal of real external danger; the text is about fear born of a sense of separateness
cautions: For someone frightened because they are actually isolated or unsafe, 'fear comes from a second' could sound like blaming the other person or minimising danger
speaks_to: fear of threats that may be imagined
not_for: someone in real danger from another person
acute loneliness needing company rather than insight

verified_ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 1.4.3 (Kanva), first half. Same in Madhavananda, Hume, Vasu/Madhva.
attribution_note: Narrative; only the 'half of a split pea' line is credited to Yajnavalkya. Speaker label is fine.
translation_note: Fair. 'Each of us is like a half' renders ardha-bṛgalam, half of a split pea (Madhavananda/Hume). Our text stops before the verse's last words: he united with her, and from that humans were born.
context: Just after the first being overcame fear (1.4.2), he finds no joy in being alone, wishes for a mate, and splits his own body in two to make husband and wife. The verse continues with their union and the birth of humans, then the wife hides in animal forms and the creation of all pairs follows (1.4.4).

key_terms.sense: this space is filled by the wife

core_teaching: The longing for a partner is built into embodied life from the first being onward; the couple is pictured as two halves of one whole. Shankara adds that this shows even the first being was still within desire.

commentaries.gist: Viraj's unease shows he is within the relative world. To end it he desired a wife and projected a body the size of man and wife together, then split it, so each partner is half of oneself.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu, SBH vol. 14 (1916)
commentaries.gist: Brahma, alone, felt no delight and wished for a wife; his body held Sarasvati within it, the size of both together, and he then divided it.

practical_reading: Wanting closeness is not a weakness; the text treats it as basic to being human. Teachers also use it to ask whether we expect another person to complete us.
misreadings: Not a claim that unmarried people are incomplete or less
Not a rule that a wife exists to fill a man's space; the original is male-centred and should be read gender-neutrally
cautions: Heteronormative and male-centred framing ('space filled by the wife')
Can sting for the widowed, divorced or involuntarily single if read as 'you are only half'
not_for: recently widowed or divorced readers
people who feel judged for being single

verified_ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 1.4.16 (Kanva), middle part. Same in Madhavananda and Hume.
attribution_note: No speaker; narrator is fine.
translation_note: Accurate for the part given, but partial and missing the frame: the verse says 'this self is a world (loka) for all beings' and first lists offerings to gods, Vedic study for the sages, and offerings and children for the ancestors before the lines we quote. It ends: just as one wishes safety for one's own body, all beings wish safety for one who knows this.
context: After the creation story, 1.4.15-16 describe the householder's life of ritual duty. Each regular duty makes him a 'world', a support, for some class of beings: gods, sages, ancestors, humans, animals, down to ants. Shankara stresses this describes the ritual householder who has not yet known the Self; 1.4.17 turns to desire as what drives such a life.

key_terms.sense: a world; here, a support or source of sustenance for others

core_teaching: By sheltering people, feeding guests and providing for animals, a household becomes a support for all beings, and all beings in turn wish it well.

commentaries.gist: The ritual householder, still identified with body and organs, sustains every class of beings through his duties: sacrifice for gods, study for sages, offspring for ancestors, food and shelter for people, fodder for animals.

practical_reading: Ordinary hospitality and care for animals make a home a small world others live by; feeding a guest or a stray is part of a spiritual life, not separate from it.
misreadings: Not 'give so that you are praised'
Not the Upanishad's final word on the good life: Shankara frames it as the ritual householder's path, below Self-knowledge
cautions: Framed around a male householder; keep it gender-neutral
speaks_to: feeling one's daily care work is small
not_for: someone already overburdened by caring for others who needs permission to rest
research_note: Only one classical commentary read for this verse (Madhva's reading in SBH vol. 14 not checked).

verified_ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.4.2 (Kanva; repeated almost word for word at 4.5.3). Same number in Madhavananda, Hume and Vasu/Madhva.
attribution_note: Dialogue: Maitreyi asks, Yajnavalkya answers. Correct.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Like the life of the well-off' = upakaraṇavatām, people well supplied with things (Madhva's translator: furniture and possessions).
context: Yajnavalkya is about to leave home for the wandering life and offers to settle his property between his two wives, Maitreyi and Katyayani (2.4.1). Maitreyi asks whether a whole earth full of wealth would make her immortal. He says no, and she then asks for what he knows instead (2.4.3), opening his teaching on the Self.

key_terms.sense: the life of people well supplied with things
there is no hope of immortality through wealth

core_teaching: Wealth can make life comfortable but cannot give what is deathless; not even the hope of it comes through money.

commentaries.gist: Maitreyi asks whether rites paid for with the whole earth's wealth could make her immortal. Yajnavalkya: her life would just be like the well-provided; wealth and its works give no hope of immortality.

practical_reading: A clear question to ask of any big goal: will this give me what I really want, or only a more comfortable version of the same life?
misreadings: Not a condemnation of earning or having money
Not a promise that renouncing wealth by itself brings freedom
cautions: For someone in financial distress, 'wealth doesn't matter' can sound glib; the verse is about its limits, not its uselessness
not_for: someone in poverty or debt crisis
research_note: Madhva's text for this verse was read (translation only); no distinct Madhva gloss found for it, so only one commentary is listed.

verified_ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.4.3 (Kanva; parallel 4.5.4).
attribution_note: Maitreyi to Yajnavalkya. Correct.
translation_note: Accurate.
context: Maitreyi has just been told that wealth gives no hope of immortality. She sets the property aside and asks for what he knows. In the next verse Yajnavalkya says she was dear to him and now speaks what is dearer still, and he begins the teaching that all things are dear for the sake of the Self.

key_terms.sense: that by which I would not become immortal
what would I do with it?
just what you, revered one, know

core_teaching: Once you see something cannot give what matters most, set it down and ask for the real thing.

commentaries.gist: Since wealth will not make her immortal, Maitreyi asks what use it is, and requests only what Yajnavalkya knows to be the sole means of immortality.

practical_reading: Before taking a settlement, a promotion or a comfortable option, ask what you actually want from it, and ask the people who know.
misreadings: Not a model of a wife rejecting her rights or inheritance in general
Not contempt for practical provision
cautions: Maitreyi's choice is often held up as an ideal for women to give up property; frame it as her own free intellectual choice
speaks_to: a decision point between comfort and meaning
wanting real answers rather than consolation
not_for: someone being pressured to give up money or rights they need
research_note: Only Shankara's gloss was read; it is brief.

verified_ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.4.5 (Kanva; parallel 4.5.6). Our text gives only the first three of the verse's many clauses (husband, wife, sons); the verse continues with wealth, brahmins, kshatriyas, worlds, gods, beings and 'all', and ends: the Self is to be seen, heard about, reflected on and meditated on.
attribution_note: Yajnavalkya to Maitreyi. Correct.
translation_note: The clauses given are accurate but the verse is cut before its point, the instruction to know the Self (ātmā vā are draṣṭavyaḥ śrotavyo mantavyo nididhyāsitavyaḥ). The truncation makes it read as a cynical claim that all love is selfish, which no commentator intends.
context: Maitreyi has asked for the teaching that leads to immortality. Yajnavalkya explains that every dear thing is dear for the sake of the Self, so the Self is what must be heard of, reflected on and realised; knowing it, all is known. The following verses give images of the drum, conch and lute, whose sounds are grasped by grasping the instrument.

key_terms.sense: for the sake of the Self
to be seen, heard of, reflected on, meditated upon

core_teaching: What we love in any person or thing is, at bottom, the Self; so the Self is the primary object of love and the one thing to come to know.

commentaries.gist: Meant to build dispassion for renunciation: spouse, sons and wealth are loved for one's own sake, so love of them is secondary and love of the Self primary. Hence hear of, reflect on and meditate on the Self.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu, SBH vol. 14 (1916)
commentaries.gist: Madhva explicitly rejects reading this as selfish love. 'Atman' here is the Lord Narayana: husband and wife become dear to each other only by his will, which is why mere wishing cannot make someone love us.

practical_reading: Love points beyond the person to something deeper we share with them; teachers use it to loosen possessiveness and to look for what we are really seeking in our relationships.
misreadings: Not 'all love is selfish, so people don't really love you'
Not a reason to withdraw affection from family
cautions: Easy to quote as cynical about love; always include or paraphrase the closing instruction about knowing the Self
Hurts in a failing marriage or after betrayal if read as 'your partner only used you'
speaks_to: asking what we really seek in relationships
not_for: someone just betrayed or abandoned
a parent estranged from a child

verified_ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 3.5.1 (Kanva), second half (Kahola Brahmana). Same in Madhavananda, Hume, Müller SBE 15, Vasu/Madhva.
attribution_note: Yajnavalkya answering Kahola Kaushitakeya. Speaker/listener correct.
translation_note: Disputed key word. Our 'live like a child' / 'childlike simplicity' follows Müller, Hume and Deussen for bālya. Both Shankara and Madhva read bālya as 'strength' (from bala): Shankara, the strength of Self-knowledge; Madhva, strength of reasoning. Müller's footnote flags the passage as obscure and possibly corrupt. Our `line` and `our_note` follow Shankara, so translation and note disagree. Suggest: 'should rest in the strength that comes from knowing (some translate: live like a child)'. Also: the verse opens with Kahola's question about the Self within all, and the first half says the Self is beyond hunger, thirst, grief, delusion, old age and death.
context: At King Janaka's debate Kahola asks Yajnavalkya to explain the Brahman that is immediate and direct, the Self within all. Yajnavalkya says it is beyond hunger, thirst, grief, delusion, old age and death; knowing it, sages drop the desires for sons, wealth and worlds and live by begging. The verse ends: however such a knower behaves, he is just that; all else is perishable. Kahola falls silent.

key_terms.sense: contested: 'childlikeness' (Müller, Hume) or 'strength' of knowledge (Shankara, Madhva)
silence; the meditative state of a muni

core_teaching: The drives for children, money and status are one craving in different forms; the knower drops them and passes through learning, inner strength or simplicity, and silence to direct knowledge.

commentaries.gist: Having mastered Self-knowledge from teacher and scripture, the knower renounces desires and lives on the strength that knowledge gives, so the senses cannot drag him; then becomes meditative; then a true knower. Shankara uses the passage to defend full renunciation.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu, SBH vol. 14 (1916)
commentaries.gist: After acquiring learning one should establish oneself in the strength of reasoning, then become a muni; passing through meditation and beyond it, one becomes a direct knower. Whatever his condition, such a one stays a beggar for God's grace.

Gives the 'become as a child' reading (after Gough and Deussen) but doubts 'knowledge of babes' is an Indian idea, notes Shankara reads it otherwise elsewhere (Vedanta Sutra 3.4.50), and suspects the text may be corrupt.

practical_reading: Wanting children, money and recognition can all be the same restless reaching; teachers use it to invite simplicity, learning that turns into stillness, and less need to prove oneself.
misreadings: Not a command for householders to abandon family
Not anti-intellectual: learning is the first step, not something to skip
'Like a child' does not mean naive or irresponsible
cautions: Lumping the wish for children with greed can hurt people struggling to have children
Renunciation context (begging monks) needs framing for lay readers
not_for: someone grieving infertility
someone whose financial worry is about survival

verified_ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 3.8.2 (Kanva). Same in Madhavananda and Hume.
attribution_note: Gargi Vachaknavi to Yajnavalkya. Correct. In 3.8.1 she first asks the assembly's leave to put two questions.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Warrior' renders ugraputra, son of a warrior line; the bow is strung and the two arrows are bamboo-tipped and deadly to foes.
context: This is Gargi's second time on her feet in the debate (in 3.6 Yajnavalkya stopped her from asking too far). She asks the brahmins' permission, then compares her two questions to a warrior's arrows. She asks what space is woven on, and he answers: the Imperishable (akshara), which he then describes by negations (3.8.8).
core_teaching: Gargi frames her questions as a direct challenge, warrior-style; the scene honours searching, fearless questioning in a public assembly.

commentaries.gist: With the assembly's leave, Gargi uses the image of a valiant archer of Kashi or Videha holding two deadly arrows to show her questions will be very hard, and dares him to answer if he knows Brahman.

practical_reading: Readers use Gargi as a model of courage in asking hard questions, especially for women speaking up where they are outnumbered.
misreadings: Not hostility for its own sake: her aim is to test whether the teacher truly knows
Not a story of a woman 'put in her place': she ends by declaring him unbeatable on her own judgment
speaks_to: speaking up in a room that doubts you
preparing for a tough interview or exam
not_for: someone looking for comfort rather than challenge
research_note: Only Shankara read for this verse.

verified_ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 3.8.10 (Kanva). Same in Madhavananda and Hume.
attribution_note: Yajnavalkya to Gargi. Correct.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Pitiable' renders kṛpaṇa (Madhavananda: miserable; Shankara likens it to a slave bought for a price). 'True knower' renders brāhmaṇa.
context: Yajnavalkya has just described the Imperishable as the ruler under whose command sun and moon, earth and sky, days and years keep their places (3.8.9). Here he adds that ritual and austerity without knowing it end in finite results, and that knowing it makes one a brahmana. Next he calls it the unseen seer, unheard hearer (3.8.11).
core_teaching: Even thousands of years of worship and austerity come to an end; only knowing the imperishable gives a result that does not run out.

commentaries.gist: The Imperishable must exist, since knowing it ends transmigration and rites alone cannot. Rites yield results that are used up; one who dies without this knowledge is pitiable like a bought slave, while one who knows it is a brahmana.

practical_reading: Busy effort, even religious effort, is not the same as understanding; it invites a reader to ask what all their striving rests on.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of ritual or service as worthless; Shankara says they give real but finite results
'Pitiable' is about missing the goal, not a judgment on a person's worth
cautions: Speaks of dying without knowledge as pitiable: avoid for someone whose loved one has just died
not_for: recently bereaved readers
someone with scrupulosity who fears they are 'doing it wrong'
research_note: Only Shankara read.

verified_ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 3.8.12 (Kanva), last verse of the Gargi Brahmana.
attribution_note: Gargi to the assembled brahmins. Correct.
translation_note: Accurate in sense. 'Get away from him with a bow' = escape by saluting him (namaskāreṇa); 'talk about Brahman' = brahmodya, the formal debate on Brahman.
context: Yajnavalkya has just answered Gargi's second question: space is woven on the Imperishable, the unseen seer. Gargi now turns to the brahmins and tells them to be glad if they can leave with a bow, since no one will beat him. She falls silent. Next Vidagdha Shakalya presses him regardless (3.9) and meets a grim end.

key_terms.sense: get off by just bowing to him

core_teaching: Gargi, having tested Yajnavalkya herself, publicly concedes his mastery and counsels her peers to accept it.

commentaries.gist: Gargi tells the brahmins to count themselves lucky to escape with a salute; they should not even think of defeating him, since she already said that if he answered her two questions nobody could. Then she stopped.

practical_reading: Knowing when you have met someone who knows more, and saying so openly, is a strength; it also models honest concession after a fair test.
misreadings: Not a story of Gargi being defeated or silenced: her silence follows her own verdict
cautions: The next section (3.9.26) ends with a rival's head falling apart; do not pair it with that
not_for: someone already feeling humiliated or outclassed
research_note: Only Shankara read.

verified_ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 3.9.28, the fourth of seven verses grouped under 3.9.28 (cited as 3.9.28.4 or 3.9.28(4)). Same in Madhavananda and Hume.
attribution_note: Yajnavalkya to the brahmins. Correct.
translation_note: Accurate.
context: After Shakalya's fatal failure (3.9.26), Yajnavalkya challenges the silent brahmins in verse. He maps a person's body onto a tree (hair as leaves, skin as bark, blood as sap), then asks: a felled tree sprouts again from its root, but from what root does a person grow again after death? He rules out 'from seed' and says a tree pulled up by its root does not return. No one can answer, and the Upanishad gives its own reply: Brahman, knowledge and bliss.

key_terms.sense: a mortal cut down by death
Brahman, knowledge and bliss (the answer in verse 7)

core_teaching: The riddle points to a root of life that death does not reach; the text's answer is Brahman, consciousness and bliss.

commentaries.gist: Person and tree match, except a felled tree sprouts again and a dead man is not seen to. Yet he must arise from some root; the brahmins could not name it; the text names Brahman, knowledge and bliss.

practical_reading: Teachers use the image to ask what in us is deeper than what can be cut away; it is often read at the end of life as a question rather than an answer.
misreadings: Not a promise that the person will literally come back
Out of context it reads as a bleak riddle; the text's own answer follows
cautions: Directly about death and being 'cut down'; Shankara reads it in terms of rebirth, which can feel dismissive in fresh grief
Comes right after a debater's head 'falls apart' in the text
not_for: fresh grief
someone with suicidal thoughts
research_note: Madhva's gloss read only for the first verse of the sequence (tree and person); not counted for this verse.

verified_ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 4.2.1 (Kanva). Same in Madhavananda and Hume.
attribution_note: Dialogue between Yajnavalkya and Janaka, Emperor of Videha. Correct. The verse opens with Janaka coming down from his seat and asking to be taught.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Equipped yourself with these teachings' renders upaniṣadbhiḥ samāhitātmā: Shankara, you have furnished your mind with many secret names (meditations) on Brahman.
context: In 4.1 Janaka told Yajnavalkya what six teachers had taught him, and Yajnavalkya showed each was only a partial definition of Brahman. Now the king leaves his seat, bows and asks for teaching. Yajnavalkya points out that for all his learning and wealth he does not know where he goes after death, and begins the teaching on the self in the heart, ending by declaring Janaka has reached fearlessness (4.2.4).

key_terms.sense: about to set out on a long journey

core_teaching: Gathering teachings, honours and wealth is like fitting out a vehicle; it is no use if you do not know your destination.

commentaries.gist: Janaka drops his pride and bows. Yajnavalkya says he has fitted his mind with many meditations on Brahman like a traveller's chariot or boat, and is rich and learned, yet lacking Self-knowledge he does not know his destination.

practical_reading: Credentials, reading and success are equipment; the verse asks whether you know what they are for. The king's humility in admitting 'I do not know' is the turning point.
misreadings: Not contempt for learning or wealth: they are the vehicle, just not the destination
cautions: 'When you leave this world' is about death; light to moderate
speaks_to: someone who has read a lot but feels stuck
not_for: someone facing imminent death of a loved one, if the 'where will you go' line is quoted bare
research_note: Only Shankara gives a verse-level gloss here; Krishnananda's chapter introduction (read) is general.

verified_ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 4.3.5-6 (Kanva); the series begins at 4.3.2 (sun) and 4.3.3-4 (moon, fire). Same in Madhavananda and Hume.
attribution_note: Janaka asks, Yajnavalkya answers. Correct.
translation_note: Accurate; 4.3.5 and 4.3.6 are merged. 'Speech' (vāk) means sound in general, per Shankara.
context: Janaka asks what light a person has. Yajnavalkya answers in steps: the sun; when it sets, the moon; then fire; then speech (sound you can follow in the dark); and finally the self. Janaka then asks 'which is the self?' and is told it is the light within the heart, made of consciousness (4.3.7), leading into the long teaching on waking, dream and deep sleep.

key_terms.sense: what light does a person have?
the self alone is his light

core_teaching: When every outer light and sign fails, a person still sits, moves and acts by an inner light, the self, which is distinct from body and senses.

commentaries.gist: Sound guides us in the dark, so speech serves as light. When even that stops, as in dream and sleep, a light distinct from body and senses still works: the self, which lights everything and is lit by nothing.

practical_reading: In the darkest periods, when the usual supports and signals are gone, something in us still knows and keeps going; teachers use it to point to that inner witness.
misreadings: Not a claim that outer help is useless: the text values each outer light in turn
not_for: someone needing practical help now, if offered as a substitute for it
research_note: Only Shankara read.

verified_ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 4.4.3 (Kanva). Same in Madhavananda, Hume, Müller SBE 15, Vasu/Madhva.
attribution_note: Yajnavalkya to Janaka. Correct.
translation_note: Two issues. (1) 'Let go of ignorance' follows Müller and Hume ('dispelled its ignorance') but Shankara reads avidyāṃ gamayitvā as 'making the body senseless', and our own our_note says so; translation and note contradict each other. Madhva reads it as the Lord making the soul understand ignorance. (2) The creature (tṛṇajalāyukā) is a leech in Shankara and Madhva, a caterpillar in Müller and Hume; both are acceptable. Suggest: 'having let this body go and left it senseless'.
context: 4.4 describes dying. In 4.4.1-2 the senses gather into the heart, the self leaves by the eye or head or another opening, and knowledge, deeds and past impressions take hold of it. Here the leech image shows the self reaching the next body before leaving the last; 4.4.4 adds the goldsmith image; 4.4.5-6 say one becomes according to one's desires and deeds.

key_terms.sense: leech (or caterpillar) on a blade of grass
taking hold of the next support
disputed: making (the body) senseless (Shankara) / dispelling ignorance (Müller, Hume)

core_teaching: At death the self, carried by its impressions, already reaches toward a new embodiment before leaving the old, as a leech grips the next blade of grass.

commentaries.gist: As a leech grips the next straw before letting go, the transmigrating self casts off this body, makes it senseless, reaches the next body through its impressions and identifies with it, as it makes a dream body.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu, SBH vol. 14 (1916)
commentaries.gist: It is the Lord who removes the soul from the gross body by grasping its subtle body, and who gives the soul knowledge so it understands ignorance; the leech image applies to souls nearing release as well.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to say life is continuous and that our habits and wishes shape what comes next; some apply it to transitions within a life (we tend to grab the next thing before letting go).
misreadings: Not a statement that the dying person has already 'moved on' and so needs no care
The second line does not mean the dead are freed from ignorance (Shankara reads it as the body made senseless)
cautions: Explicitly about death and rebirth; can feel dismissive or frightening in fresh grief
Avoid for readers caring for a dying relative unless they ask about death
speaks_to: questions about what happens at death
making peace with mortality in later life
not_for: fresh bereavement
someone with suicidal thoughts
parents who have lost a child

verified_ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 4.4.4 (Kanva). Same in Madhavananda, Hume, Müller SBE 15.
attribution_note: Yajnavalkya to Janaka. Correct.
translation_note: Same issue as 4.4.3: 'letting go of ignorance' (Müller/Hume) vs Shankara's 'making the body senseless'; our_note follows Shankara. Also our translation drops the end of the verse: the new form is that of ancestors, gandharvas, gods, Prajapati, Brahma or other beings, according to one's deeds and knowledge (Shankara). 'Goldsmith' (peśaskārī) is the standard rendering.
context: Continues the account of dying. After the leech image (4.4.3), this verse explains how the self makes a new body: as a goldsmith reworks the same gold into a newer, finer shape, the self reworks the same elements. The next verses say one becomes what one desires and does, and that the one free of desire does not go anywhere but becomes Brahman (4.4.6-7).
core_teaching: The self keeps reshaping the same elements into new bodies, finer or not, according to its past deeds and understanding.

commentaries.gist: As a goldsmith reworks the same gold, the self repeatedly reworks the five ever-present elements into another, newer form suited to ancestors, celestial singers, gods, Viraj, Hiranyagarbha or other beings, depending on its past work and knowledge.

practical_reading: Often used hopefully: what we are can be refashioned into something better. Teachers add that what shapes the new form is how we live and what we understand now.
misreadings: Not a guarantee that the next life is 'more beautiful' for everyone: the form depends on deeds and knowledge
Not a reason to treat this life or body as disposable
cautions: About death and rebirth; the 'newer and more beautiful' line can sound like a platitude to the newly bereaved
speaks_to: later stages of grief, when consolation is welcome
not_for: fresh grief
someone with suicidal thoughts
research_note: Only Shankara read in full; Madhva's gloss not checked for this verse.

verified_ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 4.4.12 (Kanva), a verse (shloka) within the closing verses of 4.4. Same in Madhavananda and Hume.
attribution_note: Within Yajnavalkya's teaching to Janaka; the verses are quoted, not composed for the dialogue. Fine.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Fret after the body' = śarīram anusañjvaret, suffer along with the body's fevers.
context: After explaining that the one without desires does not go anywhere but becomes Brahman (4.4.6-7), Yajnavalkya cites a series of verses on the knower. This one says that once a person knows 'I am this', there is nothing left to crave on the body's behalf. The verses that follow praise the wonder of awakening in 'this dense jungle' of the body (4.4.13).

key_terms.sense: burn with fever after the body, suffer with it

core_teaching: Craving and the suffering that follows the body's ups and downs depend on not knowing who we are; with that knowledge, there is nothing missing to chase.

commentaries.gist: 'If' marks how rare this is. Knowing oneself as the one Self of all, there is nothing outside to want and no one else to want it for, so one no longer suffers along with the body.

commentaries.who: Swami Krishnananda (Divine Life Society), discourse on the Brihadaranyaka
commentaries.gist: Birth and suffering come from desire turned outward to the non-self. If the Self is recognised in every object with the same intimacy we feel for our own being, the object stops being an object; that is liberation.

practical_reading: When you notice yourself chasing one more thing for comfort or status, ask: wanting what, for whose sake? The question itself often loosens the grip.
misreadings: Not a recommendation to neglect health or the body's needs
Not 'pain isn't real'
cautions: Can sound dismissive to someone in chronic illness or pain if read as 'stop fretting over your body'
not_for: someone with serious illness or chronic pain
eating-disorder or body-image struggles

verified_ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 4.4.14 (Kanva). Same in Madhavananda and Hume.
attribution_note: Quoted verse within Yajnavalkya's teaching. Fine.
translation_note: Two readings exist. Hume (and our text) read the first line as 'while we are here we may know it'; Shankara reads it as thanksgiving: 'being in this body we have somehow known it; had we not, the loss would have been great', and our_note follows Shankara. Either is defensible; note the difference.
context: Part of the closing verses of 4.4 on the knower. The preceding verse speaks of the one who has awakened to the Self in this body; this one says the chance is here and now, and missing it is a great loss. The following verses describe the Self as lord of past and future, beyond fear.

key_terms.sense: being right here, in this life

core_teaching: This life is the opportunity to know the Self; not using it is the great loss.

commentaries.gist: Read as thanksgiving: in this body, under ignorance's long sleep, we have somehow known Brahman; otherwise endless birth and death would follow. Knowers become immortal; those who take the body as self get sorrow.

commentaries.who: Swami Krishnananda (Divine Life Society), discourse on the Brihadaranyaka
commentaries.gist: The body is given as a vehicle for moving toward God; if it is used only for the senses and this world is taken as all, life has been wasted and that is the great loss.

practical_reading: A nudge not to postpone what matters most; teachers read it as urgency about inner life, not fear.
misreadings: Not a threat of damnation
Not a judgment that people who die without spiritual knowledge are doomed
cautions: 'Great loss' and 'go only to sorrow' can wound someone recently bereaved or anxious about a loved one's death
Can feed scrupulosity or spiritual anxiety
not_for: fresh grief
anxious or perfectionistic readers

verified_ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 4.4.21 (Kanva). Same in Madhavananda and Hume.
attribution_note: Quoted verse within Yajnavalkya's teaching. Fine.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Seeker' renders brāhmaṇa; 'cultivate understanding' = prajñāṃ kurvīta.
context: Near the end of the closing verses of 4.4. Having described the Self as unborn and beyond measure, the text advises the seeker to turn knowledge into direct insight and not get lost in endless words. 4.4.22 follows with the great description of the Self as the lord of all, untouched by good or bad deeds, sought through study, sacrifice, giving and austerity.

key_terms.sense: should not dwell on many words

core_teaching: Once you have understood the teaching, practise it into insight; more words only tire you.

commentaries.gist: Having learned of the Self from teacher and scripture, the seeker should make it direct insight by practising renunciation, calm, self-control, withdrawal, endurance and concentration. A few words on the Self's unity are fine; many words only tire the voice.

commentaries.who: Swami Krishnananda (Divine Life Society), discourse on the Brihadaranyaka
commentaries.gist: Like a mother's advice: don't read or talk too much in the later stages, it drains energy. Some study is needed at first, but practice should follow correct understanding, and much of life may go into understanding the goal properly.

practical_reading: After a point, more books, podcasts and debate become a way to avoid practice; choose one thing you understand and live it.
misreadings: Not anti-learning: understanding comes first
Not a ban on conversation or asking questions
not_for: a beginner who needs to learn more first

verified_ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 4.4.23 (Kanva), the last verse of Yajnavalkya's teaching in 4.4. Same in Madhavananda and Hume.
attribution_note: Yajnavalkya to Janaka, quoting a Rig-style verse. Correct.
translation_note: Accurate for the part given. The verse continues: evil does not overcome him, he overcomes all evil; he becomes sinless, stainless, free of doubt; 'this is the world of Brahman, O king, and you have reached it'. Janaka then offers his kingdom and himself in service.
context: This seals the long teaching to Janaka. It quotes a verse that the knower's greatness neither grows by good deeds nor shrinks by bad, and from that draws the five qualities (calm, self-controlled, withdrawn, patient, collected) in which one sees the Self everywhere. Janaka responds by offering Yajnavalkya the kingdom of Videha and himself as servant.

key_terms.sense: neither grows by action nor becomes less

core_teaching: The worth of one who knows the Self does not depend on deeds; from that security come calm, restraint, patience and steadiness, and one sees the Self in all.

commentaries.gist: Other glories come from work and pass; this one is natural and eternal, unchanged by good or bad work. Knowing it, one becomes calm, controlled, desireless, enduring and concentrated, and sees all as the Self.

practical_reading: Your basic worth is not up for grabs in every success or failure; resting in that makes it easier to be patient, calm and focused.
misreadings: Not a licence to act badly because 'deeds don't touch the knower'
Not a claim that effort and ethics don't matter: the five disciplines are the practice
cautions: 'Not stained by wrong action' can be misused to excuse harm; present with its ethical frame
not_for: someone looking to excuse harm they have done
research_note: Only Shankara read.

verified_ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 5.1.1 (Kanva). The first half (pūrṇam adaḥ...) is also the shanti-patha of the Isha Upanishad and the Shukla Yajurveda. Same in Madhavananda and Hume.
attribution_note: No speaker for the first half; the second half quotes the son of Kauravyayani. Fine.
translation_note: Accurate. Madhavananda renders pūrṇa as 'infinite'; 'whole' and 'full' are both standard.
context: Book 5 opens a supplement after the main teaching of Books 1-4. It begins with the famous verse on fullness and then gives a meditation on Om as space (kha). It is followed by the 'Da Da Da' teaching (5.2) and other meditations.
core_teaching: The source and what comes from it are both whole; nothing is lost when the world arises from the infinite, and the infinite alone remains.

commentaries.gist: 'That' is the unconditioned Brahman, 'this' the same Brahman appearing through name and form; both are infinite. The effect comes from the cause without losing infinitude; when its apparent separateness is removed by knowledge, the one infinite alone remains.

commentaries.who: Swami Krishnananda (Divine Life Society), discourse on the Brihadaranyaka
commentaries.gist: From fullness only fullness can come: the whole cosmos is reflected in every particle, and the Absolute loses nothing when the universe emerges, unlike any physical source that is depleted by what it gives.

practical_reading: Recited as a peace chant: you are not a fragment cut off from the whole, and giving does not diminish what is truly full.
misreadings: Not a mathematical claim; 'whole minus whole' is a pointer, not arithmetic

verified_ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 5.2.1-3 (Kanva). Same in Madhavananda, Hume, Vasu/Madhva.
attribution_note: Prajapati teaches gods, humans and asuras. Correct. Madhva identifies Prajapati as Brahma.
translation_note: Accurate and complete.
context: In the supplement to the Upanishad, after the verse on fullness and the meditation on Om, comes this short parable. Each group of Prajapati's children, after their studentship, gets the same single syllable 'Da' and hears in it the lesson they most need. The thunder still repeats it. 5.3 then turns to the heart (hṛdaya) as Brahman.
core_teaching: One syllable, three lessons: restraint, giving and compassion. Each hearer took the one they lacked, and every person should learn all three.

commentaries.gist: Gods are unruly, humans greedy, asuras cruel, so each heard the lesson for its own fault. All three faults exist in people, so all should learn restraint, giving and compassion; awareness of a fault makes a hint enough.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. S. C. Vasu, SBH vol. 14 (1916)
commentaries.gist: Madhva reads dama for the gods as humility, not letting power and lordliness make them proud; humans are to give, asuras to be merciful. All beings should practise all three to grow in merit.

practical_reading: Hear the same advice and notice which part stings: that is probably yours. A simple daily check: where do I need restraint, generosity and kindness today?
misreadings: Not 'some people are demons': the three types are tendencies in everyone
Not three separate lessons for three groups only; the text says to learn all three
speaks_to: family or team where each person needs different advice

verified_ref: Chandogya Upanishad 1.1.10 (Shankara/Jha and standard numbering). Madhva's edition (Vasu) numbers this as 1.1.8.
attribution_note: No speaker; the verse is framed as an objection and its answer. Fine.
translation_note: Accurate, but the context is narrow: 'the act' is the Vedic rite using the syllable Om/Udgitha, and the verse ends 'this is the explanation of this very syllable'. Our generalised reading ('whatever is done with knowledge...') is the standard application but should be marked as such. Upaniṣad is glossed by Shankara as yoga/concentration; Madhva as acting according to one's capacity.
context: The Chandogya opens with meditation on Om as the Udgitha, the essence of all essences. After explaining its meaning, the text raises an objection: both the one who understands Om and the one who doesn't perform the rite with it, so why learn? The answer: knowing and not knowing differ, and what is done with knowledge, faith and concentration is stronger. This closes the first section.

key_terms.sense: but knowledge and ignorance are different

core_teaching: The same outward act carries more power when done with understanding, faith and focused attention.

commentaries.gist: Against the objection that a medicine works whether understood or not: a merchant who knows gems gets a better price than a forest dweller selling the same stones. Acts done with knowledge, faith and concentration bear more fruit.

(His 1.1.8.) Both the wise and the ignorant should perform the worship, but knowledge and ignorance differ: worship of the Lord with knowledge, faith and propriety leads to endless reward, that of the ignorant to limited reward.

practical_reading: Doing the same daily task with understanding and wholehearted attention changes what it yields; it encourages knowing why you do what you do.
misreadings: Not 'only experts should act': both perform the act, the text says
Not a magic formula: 'more powerful' refers to the fruit of a rite done with understanding
speaks_to: going through the motions at work or in prayer
not_for: someone already crushed by perfectionism about 'doing it right'

verified_ref: Chandogya Upanishad 3.14.1 (the Shandilya Vidya). Same in Jha and Madhva/Vasu.
attribution_note: Teaching ascribed to Shandilya at 3.14.4; 'Shandilya' is correct.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Resolve' renders kratu (Jha: volition; Shankara: firm conviction, decision). 'From it all arises, into it dissolves, in it breathes' renders the compressed word tajjalān.
context: Chapter 3 has been teaching meditations on the sun and on Gayatri. Here begins Shandilya's meditation: all this is Brahman, and a person becomes after death what their settled conviction is here. The next verses describe what to meditate on: the self in the heart, smaller than a grain of rice yet greater than the worlds, which 'I shall reach on departing' (3.14.2-4).

key_terms.sense: born from it, dissolving in it, living in it
a person is made of resolve, conviction

core_teaching: Everything rises from, lives in and returns to Brahman; and since a person becomes what they firmly resolve, one should settle the right conviction calmly.

commentaries.gist: The world is Brahman because at origin, life and dissolution it is never found apart from it. Meditate calmly, free of love and hate. Volition is firm conviction; as it is here, so one becomes after death.

The Lord in the heart is the same Lord who pervades the universe: smaller than the atomic soul, greater than the cosmos. 'All this' (sarvam) names him as possessing all qualities; tajjalān names Vishnu who moves on the waters.

practical_reading: What you repeatedly settle on in your mind shapes who you become; choose your convictions deliberately and hold them calmly.
misreadings: Not 'think positive and you'll get what you want'
'All is Brahman' is not a reason to ignore wrongs in the world
cautions: 'So one becomes on departing' links conviction to after-death state; can worry readers anxious about a loved one's last thoughts
speaks_to: wanting a sense of the sacred in everything
not_for: someone obsessing that their thoughts cause bad events

verified_ref: Chandogya Upanishad 3.17.4. Same in Jha and Madhva/Vasu.
attribution_note: The teaching of 3.17 is credited (3.17.6) to Ghora Angirasa, taught to Krishna son of Devaki. Correct.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Discipline' renders tapas (austerity); 'gifts to the priests' = dakshina, the sacrificial fee.
context: 3.16-17 treat a person's whole life as a Soma sacrifice: hunger and thirst are the initiation, eating and enjoying are the intermediate rites, laughing and loving are the chants, and these five virtues are the priests' fee. Death is the final purificatory bath (3.17.5). Ghora Angirasa taught this to Krishna, son of Devaki, who then became free of thirst (3.17.6).

key_terms.sense: the fee given to the priests that completes a sacrifice

core_teaching: If life is a sacrifice, its real offerings are discipline, generosity, honesty, non-harming and truthful speech.

commentaries.gist: These five are the fees of the life-sacrifice because, like a sacrificial fee, they strengthen the merit of the whole undertaking.
Explains the comparison of a person to a sacrifice step by step (fasting as initiation, eating as the Upasad rites, hymns, then the gifts to priests), reading the whole as a meditation on the Lord.

practical_reading: Ordinary life becomes worship when it carries these five qualities; a simple checklist for the day.
misreadings: Not a call to harsh self-denial: tapas here is discipline alongside giving and honesty
cautions: The next verse calls death the final rite of the life-sacrifice; don't pair them for the bereaved
speaks_to: people who want spirituality without ritual
research_note: Shankara's gloss on this verse is one line; Madhva's general explanation of the comparison was read, not a verse-specific gloss.

verified_ref: Chandogya Upanishad 4.4.2. Same in Jha; Madhva treats 4.4-4.9 together.
attribution_note: Jabala to her son Satyakama. Correct.
translation_note: Literal and fair; 'moved about a great deal as a serving woman' (bahv ahaṃ carantī paricāriṇī). Shankara explains it as being busy serving many guests in her husband's house and that the father died soon after. Many modern scholars read it as her not knowing the father. Our neutral wording is right; the our_note claim 'the tradition does not read unknown paternity here' is true of Shankara but should say 'Shankara does not'.
context: Satyakama wants to become a Vedic student and asks his mother his lineage (gotra), which a teacher would require. She says she doesn't know it and tells him to give his name as Satyakama Jabala, after her. He goes to Haridrumata Gautama and repeats her words exactly (4.4.3-4); the teacher accepts him for his truthfulness (4.4.5).

key_terms.sense: the mother's own name, which the son takes

core_teaching: A mother tells her son the plain truth about his uncertain origins and gives him her own name to carry; that honesty becomes his credential.

commentaries.gist: Jabala says she was too busy serving many guests in her husband's house to ask his family; she had him in her youth and his father died soon after. So he should call himself Satyakama Jabala.

Introduces the story of Satyakama (4.4-4.9) as the frame for teaching the four forms of the Lord; the gotra problem is resolved because straightforward truthfulness is taken as the sign of eligibility.

practical_reading: Telling a child the truth, even an uncomfortable one, and standing behind them gives them something sturdier than a pedigree.
misreadings: Not an occasion to moralise about the mother
Not a claim that lineage doesn't matter in the text's world: it is exactly what the teacher asks for
cautions: Touches on unknown or absent fathers and a mother's past; handle without judgment
Avoid repeating the commentators' caste reasoning (see 4.4.5)
speaks_to: adoptees and people unsure of their origins
not_for: someone being shamed about their parentage, if the reading dwells on the mother's past

verified_ref: Chandogya Upanishad 4.4.4 (with 4.4.3). Jha prints 4.4.3-4 as one unit.
attribution_note: Satyakama replying to Haridrumata Gautama. Correct.
translation_note: Accurate.

practical_reading: In families and teams, the person whose absence would hurt most is often the least noisy; it is a gentle check on ego contests.
misreadings: Not a story ranking people's worth
cautions: The test imagery is the body without life (a corpse); light

cautions: The five questions concern where people go after death

staying focused on what you need

the mind is made of food

commentaries.gist: A firefly-sized ember left from a great fire, fed with grass, can burn more than before; one of the boy's sixteen parts remained and, fed by food, blazed up so he recalled the Vedas. Mind is nourished by food.

practical_reading: When you can't think clearly, look after the body first: food, rest and care can rekindle a mind that feels empty.

attribution_note: Uddalaka to Shvetaketu. Correct.

context: 6.8 explains deep sleep: when a person sleeps, he has gone to his own (svam apīta), united with Being. The tethered bird illustrates it: the mind, tired of roaming in waking and dream, settles where it is tied. The section ends with the first 'tat tvam asi' (6.8.7).

key_terms.sense: a bird tied by a string
for the mind is tied to breath (to Being)

core_teaching: The mind roams everywhere looking for rest and finds it only where it is anchored: in deep sleep it returns to its source.

commentaries.gist: As a fowler's tethered bird flies every way and, finding no rest, settles at its tether, the mind, meaning the living self, roams through waking and dream and rests in Being (called prana here) in deep sleep.
Deep sleep shows dependence: proud of independence while awake, a person is utterly helpless in dreamless sleep, which reveals the soul's dependence on the Lord.

practical_reading: Restlessness is the mind searching; rest comes from returning to what anchors you rather than from finding a new perch.
misreadings: Not 'thinking is bad'
'Breath' is not only physiology here

verified_ref: Chandogya Upanishad 6.8.7, the first of nine occurrences of the refrain (6.8.7 to 6.16.3).
attribution_note: Uddalaka to Shvetaketu. Correct.
translation_note: Accurate on the Advaita reading. Madhva divides the words as 'atat tvam asi' ('you are not that'), a major interpretive difference the app should know about.
context: Closes the lesson on sleep, hunger, thirst and the root of the body. Having traced everything back to Being, Uddalaka states that this subtle essence is the self of all, and 'you are that'. Shvetaketu asks for more, and eight more illustrations follow (rivers, tree, seed, salt, Gandhara, the dying man, the heated axe), each ending with the same refrain.

key_terms.sense: all this has that as its self
that you are (Madhva: atat tvam asi, you are not that)

core_teaching: The fine essence underlying everything is the true self of all, and of you.

commentaries.gist: Being, the subtlest essence and source of all, is the one Self through which the universe has a self; there is no other self that transmigrates. 'You are that' tells Shvetaketu his real self is that Being.
Madhva splits the refrain as 'sa ātmā-atat tvam asi': 'you are not that'. The essence is the Lord who rules and pervades all; Shvetaketu is told he is not that God, so should drop his conceit.

practical_reading: Advaita teachers use it to say your deepest identity is not your role, body or story but the same reality as everything; Dvaita teachers use it as a lesson in humility before God.
misreadings: Not 'I am God' as ego-inflation (both schools reject that)
Not a single agreed meaning: the two major schools read it oppositely
cautions: Refrain 'tat tvam asi': Shankara reads identity of the self with Being; Madhva reads 'atat tvam asi', you are NOT that (the Lord). Present both when the refrain is used.
not_for: someone in a dissociative or depersonalised state who needs grounding

verified_ref: Chandogya Upanishad 6.10.1. Same in Jha and Madhva/Vasu.
attribution_note: Uddalaka to Shvetaketu. Correct.
translation_note: Accurate; the application to creatures and the refrain follow in 6.10.2-3.
context: After the honey image (6.9: bees' nectar from many trees cannot tell which tree it came from), the rivers flow to the sea and lose their separate names. 6.10.2 applies it: creatures that come from Being do not know they came from it, and whatever they were here (tiger, lion, wolf, insect) they become again.

key_terms.sense: from the sea they go into the sea
'I am this one' (which they no longer know)

core_teaching: Distinct names and identities merge back into one source and do not keep their separateness there.

commentaries.gist: Rivers like the Ganga and Sindhu flow east and west, are lifted from the sea by clouds and fall as rain to flow back, and once one with the ocean do not know 'I am this river or that'.

Rivers are conscious deities that cannot distinguish their own waters once in the sea; so souls entering the Lord, home of all, do not retain awareness of their lower personalities, while remaining distinct.

practical_reading: Used to ease the fear of losing oneself: differences of name and role belong to the journey, not to what we are at source.
misreadings: Not 'individuals don't matter'
cautions: Often used at funerals; for fresh grief, the loss of 'I am this river' can feel like the loss of the person
not_for: fresh grief where the mourner wants the person's individuality honoured

translation_note: Accurate. 'It is always there' (tac chaśvat saṃvartate; Jha: 'it remains for ever').

speaks_to: feeling God or meaning is absent

attribution_note: Sanatkumara to Narada. Correct.
translation_note: Acceptable. Niṣṭhā/nistiṣṭhati is rendered 'steadfast' (ours) or 'serve, be devoted' (Jha). Madhva reads the whole series as names of the Lord: 'when one knows him as Creator (kṛti), one knows him as firm'.
context: Sanatkumara leads Narada up a ladder: truth rests on understanding, understanding on thinking, thinking on faith, faith on steadfastness, steadfastness on action (kriti), action on happiness (7.22), happiness on the infinite (7.23).
core_teaching: Steady commitment comes only from doing; practice is what makes devotion firm.

commentaries.gist: Action here means restraining the senses and concentrating the mind; only when this is present do devotion and the other steps, up to true understanding, come about.
Each step names a quality of the Lord: one who knows him as Creator (kriti) knows him as firm (nishtha), and so on up the ladder.

practical_reading: Waiting to feel committed before acting gets it backwards; acting steadily builds the commitment.
misreadings: Not busyness for its own sake: Shankara reads 'action' as inner discipline
not_for: someone exhausted who needs rest more than action

verified_ref: Chandogya Upanishad 7.23.1. Same in Jha.
attribution_note: Sanatkumara to Narada. Correct.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Infinite' = bhūmā (plenitude, the vast); 'small' = alpa.
context: The summit of the ladder. Narada began (7.1) as a man who knew many texts but not the Self and was in sorrow. Sanatkumara now says happiness is only in the infinite. 7.24 defines it: where one sees, hears and knows nothing else.

key_terms.sense: to be sought to be understood

core_teaching: Lasting happiness is not in any limited thing but only in the infinite.

commentaries.gist: The finite always breeds longing for more, longing causes pain, and what causes pain is not happiness, like a fever. So there is no happiness in the small; the infinite alone, where nothing more is wanted, is happiness.
Bhuma is a name of the Lord Vishnu, the highest in the ascending series of his attributes; the bliss described is his.

practical_reading: Notice how every small satisfaction points to wanting more; the verse invites looking for contentment in something that doesn't run out.
misreadings: Not a rejection of small joys as worthless
not_for: someone in depression who can't access small joys, if it reads as 'your happiness isn't real'

verified_ref: Chandogya Upanishad 7.24.2. Same in Jha.
attribution_note: Sanatkumara to Narada. Correct.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Servants' = dāsa (Jha: slaves); 'greatness' = mahiman.
context: Narada asks what the infinite rests on. Sanatkumara says on its own greatness, or not even that. He explains: in the world, 'greatness' means owning cattle, gold, servants, wives, land and houses, one thing resting on another; he does not mean that. 7.25 then says the infinite is above, below, everywhere, and is oneself.
core_teaching: Worldly greatness always depends on possessions and other people; true greatness rests on nothing outside itself.

commentaries.gist: A person like Caitra becomes 'great' by depending on cows, horses and the like; Sanatkumara denies that the infinite rests on anything other than itself in that way.

practical_reading: Worth that depends on what you own or whom you command is borrowed; ask what your worth rests on.
misreadings: Not contempt for family or property
cautions: Lists wives and slaves among possessions; flag the historical framing
speaks_to: identity tied to wealth or a job title
after a loss of status or property
research_note: Only Shankara's verse gloss read; Madhva's section treats the series generally.

verified_ref: Chandogya Upanishad 8.3.2, second half. Same in Jha (whose index mislabels chapter 8 sections as '7.x').
attribution_note: The narrator/Upanishad (Prajapati's teaching begins only at 8.7). Listed as 'Prajapati's teaching (narrator)'; better just 'narrator'.
translation_note: Accurate for the half given. The verse's first half matters for this app: 'those of his people who are living and those who are dead, and whatever else one longs for and does not get, all that one finds by going there (into the self in the heart)'. Our text omits it.
context: 8.1-3 teach about the small space in the lotus of the heart, which contains all. 8.3.1-2 say our true desires are covered by untruth; that is why a dead relative cannot be seen. The buried treasure image follows. 8.3.3: this self is in the heart, and one who knows it goes daily to the heavenly world.

key_terms.sense: the world of Brahman (here, the self in the heart)

core_teaching: Every night in deep sleep we pass over the treasure of our own true self without finding it, because untruth, desire and ignorance carry us off.

commentaries.gist: Living and dead loved ones and all one longs for are found in the space of the heart. As people walk over buried gold unknowing, creatures enter Brahman daily in deep sleep and miss it, carried off by untruth.
The soul's true desires already exist in it and become manifest in release; they are covered over by untruth, which is why they are not realised now.

practical_reading: What you seek may be closer than you think, buried under distraction; slowing down is a way of 'knowing the spot'.
misreadings: Not 'you will literally meet your dead relatives' (though the first half is often read consolingly)
cautions: The omitted first half speaks of dead relatives being 'found' there: potentially consoling in grief but also easily over-promised
speaks_to: later stages of grief (with the first half)
not_for: fresh grief if it sounds like a promise of reunion

verified_ref: Chandogya Upanishad 8.8.4 (with 8.8.5). Same in Jha (mislabelled section '7.8' on wisdomlib).
attribution_note: Virochana to the asuras. Correct.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Body' renders ātman, which Virochana takes as the body; 'worshipped'/'tended' = mahayya/paricarya. The verse first has Prajapati remark that whoever follows this half-understanding will perish.
context: Indra and Virochana lived 32 years with Prajapati, who told them the self is what is seen in the eye; they looked at their reflections in water, dressed up, and took the body to be the self. Virochana went home satisfied and taught the asuras body-worship; 8.8.5 says that is why people who don't give or believe are called asura and adorn their dead. Indra turns back with a doubt (8.9.1).

key_terms.sense: the self (body) alone is to be glorified
the self (body) is to be tended

core_teaching: Settling for the body as the self is a half-truth that seems to work and satisfies quickly, and the Upanishad calls it the demons' doctrine.

commentaries.gist: Prajapati, seeing them leave without realising the Self, warns aloud that whoever follows this will come to grief, hoping they hear. Virochana, satisfied, preaches that the body alone is to be worshipped and served for both worlds.
The reflection gets all the body's good and bad qualities, which should have shown it is not Brahman; Virochana's failure to see this shows his ineligibility, due to impurity of heart.

practical_reading: A warning against grooming, appearance and comfort as the whole of life; it asks whether we stopped at the first satisfying answer.
misreadings: Not a rejection of caring for the body
cautions: Can be used to shame people who care about appearance or fitness
not_for: someone with body-image or eating issues if it reads as shaming

verified_ref: Chandogya Upanishad 8.9.1. Same in Jha (section mislabelled '7.9').
attribution_note: Indra thinking to himself. Correct.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Crippled' (parivṛkṇa) is rendered 'mutilated' or 'crippled'; disability language should be handled with care.
context: Indra, on his way back to the gods, realises the reflection-self shares every condition of the body, including blindness, lameness and death, and sees no good in it. He returns to Prajapati with fuel in hand (8.9.2) and is told to stay another 32 years (8.9.3).

key_terms.sense: I see no good in this

core_teaching: If you are only your body, you share all its losses and its death; seeing that clearly is the start of seeking further.

commentaries.gist: Indra, endowed with qualities like compassion, kept pondering the teaching on the way, and part of the water-pot lesson came back to him: if the reflection is the self, it must share the body's blindness and death too.
Indra actually knew the truth and only acted out the doubt, going and returning repeatedly to mislead the asuras and the ignorant.

practical_reading: A model of honest doubt: Indra doesn't settle for a comfortable answer but goes back and asks again.
misreadings: Not a claim that disabled bodies are lesser
cautions: Uses blindness and lameness as examples of loss; can hurt disabled readers
not_for: readers with disabilities if the framing is careless
someone newly injured or diagnosed

verified_ref: Chandogya Upanishad 8.9.3. Same in Jha.
attribution_note: Prajapati to Indra. Correct.
translation_note: Accurate. Indra eventually stays 101 years in all (32+32+32+5, at 8.11.3).
context: Indra returns with his doubt. Prajapati agrees, promises to explain the same self further, and asks him to live another 32 years as a student. Then he teaches the dream self (8.10), which Indra also questions; then the deep-sleep self (8.11); and finally the bodiless self (8.12).
core_teaching: The teacher affirms the student's doubt and asks for more time and preparation before going deeper.

commentaries.gist: Prajapati confirms Indra is right that the reflection is not the Self. Since Indra did not grasp what was clear to the faultless, some defect obstructs him, so he must live another 32 years as a student to remove it.
The repeated returns were Indra's choice, made knowingly so that the asuras and the ignorant would think he had not yet understood.

practical_reading: Deep understanding takes time; a good teacher honours your questions and asks you to keep going rather than handing over a quick answer.
misreadings: Not that teachers should withhold for the sake of it
not_for: someone already exhausted by endless waiting

verified_ref: Chandogya Upanishad 8.12.1. Same in Jha (section mislabelled '7.12').
attribution_note: Prajapati to Indra. Correct.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Free of the body' = aśarīra, bodiless; 'pleasure and pain' = priya and apriya.
context: After 101 years Indra receives the final teaching. The body is mortal and the dwelling of the deathless, bodiless self. While identified with the body one is held by pleasure and pain; the bodiless is untouched. 8.12.2-3: as wind and clouds rise from space and take their own form, so the serene one rises from the body and appears in its own form.
core_teaching: The body is mortal and caught in pleasure and pain; the self that dwells in it is deathless and untouched by them.

commentaries.gist: 'Held by death' means constantly seized by it, said to create detachment from the body. The body is the seat of the immortal self; embodiment is false identification, and when knowledge ends it, pleasure and pain do not touch.
The individual soul is always subject to pleasure and pain dependent on others, even in release it receives joy from God; only the bodiless Supreme Brahman is untouched, his bliss self-originated.

practical_reading: Pain and pleasure come with having a body; knowing that you are more than them can loosen their hold.
misreadings: Not a call to ignore pain or neglect health
Madhva reads 'bodiless' as God, not the individual
cautions: 'Held by death' is strong; for the terminally ill or bereaved, introduce gently
Can feel dismissive to someone in chronic pain
speaks_to: being tossed between highs and lows
not_for: someone in acute physical pain or newly diagnosed
fresh grief
